items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The self-set climate pledges that each party to the Paris Agreement (2015) must submit and update every five years"?
options: environmental defender
planetary boundaries
common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR)
nationally determined contributions (NDCs)
items.answer: nationally determined contributions (NDCs)
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of nationally determined contributions (NDCs).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement.
items.answer: Kyoto imposed top-down, legally binding targets on developed states only; Paris relies on bottom-up, voluntary NDCs from all parties, with binding procedural obligations to report and update.
items.markingKey: Kyoto imposed top-down, legally binding targets on developed states only; Paris relies on bottom-up, voluntary NDCs from all parties, with binding procedural obligations to report and update. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why pollution can be a matter of state sovereignty and interstate tension.
items.answer: Pollution crosses borders – haze from forest fires, acid rain, river contamination – so the state where it originates controls the cause while neighbours suffer the effects, as with Indonesian haze in Singapore and Malaysia.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Pollution crosses borders – haze from forest fires, acid rain, river contamination – so the state where it originates controls the cause while neighbours suffer the effects, as with Indonesian haze in Singapore and Malaysia. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source D
Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming. Global surface temperature in 2011–2020 was about 1.1°C above 1850–1900. Vulnerable communities who have historically contributed the least to current climate change are disproportionately affected.
— Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, AR6 Synthesis Report (2023) (adapted)

Identify three claims made in Source D about climate change. [3]
items.answer: human activities, mainly greenhouse gas emissions, have caused warming; temperatures in 2011–2020 were about 1.1°C above pre-industrial levels; those who contributed least are most affected
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: human activities, mainly greenhouse gas emissions, have caused warming; temperatures in 2011–2020 were about 1.1°C above pre-industrial levels; those who contributed least are most affected. items.stem:
Source C
Nature is declining globally at rates unprecedented in human history. Around one million animal and plant species are now threatened with extinction. The main drivers are changes in land and sea use, direct exploitation of organisms, climate change, pollution and invasive species.
— IPBES, Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (2019) (paraphrased)

Using evidence from Source C, explain why the source suggests biodiversity loss is a political challenge. [4]
items.answer: The drivers – land use, exploitation, pollution – result from economic and political decisions by states and firms; reversing them requires regulation, international cooperation and redistribution of costs.
items.markingKey: The drivers – land use, exploitation, pollution – result from economic and political decisions by states and firms; reversing them requires regulation, international cooperation and redistribution of costs. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Only developed countries are required to take action under the Paris Agreement." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: All parties must submit NDCs; differentiation is now self-determined, though developed states are expected to lead and provide finance.
items.markingKey: All parties must submit NDCs; differentiation is now self-determined, though developed states are expected to lead and provide finance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The voluntary approach of the Paris Agreement is too weak to address climate change." With reference to specific examples, discuss this statement. [15]
items.answer: Paris traded strength for participation; it has shifted expectations but its weak enforcement leaves a large ambition gap.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: current NDCs put the world on course for well above 1.5°C; no enforcement or penalties; major emitters can withdraw (USA 2020 and again from 2025). Arguments against: near-universal participation, unlike Kyoto; ratchet mechanism and global stocktake (2023) create peer pressure; renewable energy expansion and falling costs. Possible judgement: Paris traded strength for participation; it has shifted expectations but its weak enforcement leaves a large ambition gap. items.stem: Explain why biodiversity loss receives less political attention than climate change.
items.answer: Its effects are local, gradual and hard to measure in a single indicator, there is no single “temperature target”, and the costs fall on poorer, rural and Indigenous communities with little political voice.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Its effects are local, gradual and hard to measure in a single indicator, there is no single “temperature target”, and the costs fall on poorer, rural and Indigenous communities with little political voice. items.stem: Explain why climate change is often described as a collective action problem.
items.answer: The atmosphere is a global commons: every state benefits from reduced emissions whether or not it pays the costs, so each has an incentive to free-ride, and no world government can enforce cuts.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The atmosphere is a global commons: every state benefits from reduced emissions whether or not it pays the costs, so each has an incentive to free-ride, and no world government can enforce cuts. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to the Southeast Asian haze crisis (2015), explain how it illustrates transboundary pollution and sovereignty.
items.answer: Forest and peatland fires, many set to clear land for palm oil and pulp plantations in Indonesia, spread smoke across Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, closing schools and costing Indonesia an estimated $16 billion. The pollution originated under Indonesian sovereignty but harmed neighbours, testing the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (2002) and showing the limits of non-interference.
items.markingKey: Context (Forest and peatland fires, many set to clear land for palm oil and pulp plantations in Indonesia, spread smoke across Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, closing schools and costing Indonesia an estimated $16 billion.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The pollution originated under Indonesian sovereignty but harmed neighbours, testing the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (2002) and showing the limits of non-interference. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to transboundary pollution and sovereignty.

items.stem: Examine the view that state sovereignty is the main obstacle to effective global environmental governance. Use relevant key concepts and named examples in your answer. [15]
items.answer: Sovereignty is a major obstacle, but economic interests and inequality between states matter as much.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: states refuse binding targets (Kyoto withdrawals); non-interference blocks action on haze or deforestation; national interest in fossil fuel revenue. Arguments against: Montreal Protocol shows sovereign states can cooperate; obstacles also include corporate power and inequality; non-state actors and cities act within sovereignty. Possible judgement: Sovereignty is a major obstacle, but economic interests and inequality between states matter as much. items.stem: Why are people displaced by climate change generally not recognised as refugees under international law?
options: The 1951 Refugee Convention covers persecution on specified grounds, not environmental harm
The UNHCR has formally excluded them since 2015
They have usually not crossed a border, so the Convention does not apply
The Paris Agreement grants them a separate status
items.answer: The 1951 Refugee Convention covers persecution on specified grounds, not environmental harm
items.markingKey: A. The term “climate refugee” has no legal standing; most climate-related movement is internal.

items.stem: "Climate change directly causes civil wars." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Climate change acts as a threat multiplier; it interacts with governance, inequality and political exclusion, which remain the main drivers of conflict.
items.markingKey: Climate change acts as a threat multiplier; it interacts with governance, inequality and political exclusion, which remain the main drivers of conflict. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between resource scarcity conflict and resource abundance conflict.
items.answer: Scarcity conflicts arise from competition over declining renewable resources such as land and water (Homer-Dixon); abundance conflicts arise from valuable non-renewable resources such as oil or diamonds that finance armed groups (the resource curse).
items.markingKey: Scarcity conflicts arise from competition over declining renewable resources such as land and water (Homer-Dixon); abundance conflicts arise from valuable non-renewable resources such as oil or diamonds that finance armed groups (the resource curse). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Kiribati’s “migration with dignity” policy shows planned climate migration and sovereignty.
items.answer: Under President Anote Tong, Kiribati bought about 6,000 acres of land in Fiji (2014) and promoted skills training so that citizens could migrate as skilled workers rather than as displaced people. A vulnerable state took agency over future migration to preserve dignity and identity rather than waiting for forced displacement.
items.markingKey: Context (Under President Anote Tong, Kiribati bought about 6,000 acres of land in Fiji (2014) and promoted skills training so that citizens could migrate as skilled workers rather than as displaced people.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A vulnerable state took agency over future migration to preserve dignity and identity rather than waiting for forced displacement. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to planned climate migration and sovereignty.

items.stem:
Source A
Climate change could force up to 216 million people across six world regions to move within their countries by 2050. Hotspots of internal climate migration could emerge as early as 2030. Immediate and concerted action to reduce emissions and support green, inclusive development could reduce this scale by as much as 80 per cent.
— World Bank, Groundswell Part 2 (2021) (adapted)

Using evidence from Source A, explain why the source suggests that climate migration is a political rather than purely natural phenomenon. [4]
items.answer: It shows that the scale of migration depends on policy choices – emissions cuts and inclusive development – so migration outcomes are shaped by political decisions, not only by environmental change.
items.markingKey: It shows that the scale of migration depends on policy choices – emissions cuts and inclusive development – so migration outcomes are shaped by political decisions, not only by environmental change. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "International law should create a new legal status for climate refugees."
items.answer: A new status is morally attractive, but regional and bilateral mechanisms are more achievable and may protect more people sooner.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: existing law leaves climate migrants unprotected; Teitiota shows gaps; Pacific states face loss of territory. Arguments against: reopening the 1951 Convention could weaken protections; most movement is internal (Kampala Convention, Guiding Principles); bilateral solutions such as the Falepili Union may be more practical. Supported judgement: A new status is morally attractive, but regional and bilateral mechanisms are more achievable and may protect more people sooner.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A person forced to flee their home who has not crossed an internationally recognised border, covered by the UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement (1998)"?
options: planetary boundaries
internally displaced person (IDP)
common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR)
transnational advocacy network
items.answer: internally displaced person (IDP)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of internally displaced person (IDP).

items.stem: Briefly explain why most climate-induced migration is internal rather than international.
items.answer: Most people move short distances to nearby towns or cities, lack resources and legal routes to cross borders, and often wish to return; the World Bank projects mainly internal movement.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Most people move short distances to nearby towns or cities, lack resources and legal routes to cross borders, and often wish to return; the World Bank projects mainly internal movement. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

Source D
Claims that drought caused the Syrian civil war rest on weak evidence. The drought was not exceptional in the long term, the number of migrants was overstated, and there is little evidence that migrants played a major role in the uprising. Government policies and authoritarian rule are better explanations.

items.answer: the drought was not exceptional in the long term; the number of migrants was overstated; migrants played little role in the uprising

items.answer: Most climate-related movement is internal or regional, within the Global South, e.g. from rural Bangladesh to Dhaka.
items.markingKey: Most climate-related movement is internal or regional, within the Global South, e.g. from rural Bangladesh to Dhaka. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Misleading claims by companies or governments that their products or policies are more environmentally friendly than they really are

items.stem: Distinguish between an NGO and a social movement.
items.answer: A social movement is a loose, often informal network mobilising many people for change (Fridays for Future); an NGO is a formally organised, often professional body with staff and budgets (Greenpeace).

items.answer: NGOs range from conservation organisations working with businesses (WWF) to direct-action groups (Greenpeace) and justice-oriented networks; they often disagree on markets, offsetting and tactics.

items.stem: With reference to KlimaSeniorinnen v Switzerland (2024), explain how it illustrates climate litigation by non-state actors.
items.answer: An association of more than 2,000 older Swiss women argued that heatwaves endangered their health; the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Switzerland’s inadequate climate policy violated the right to private and family life (Article 8). A civil society group used regional human-rights law to hold a state accountable, showing how activism can create binding obligations.
items.markingKey: Context (An association of more than 2,000 older Swiss women argued that heatwaves endangered their health; the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Switzerland’s inadequate climate policy violated the right to private and family life (Article 8).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. options: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf
Wangari Maathai
Vandana Shiva
Berta Cáceres
items.answer: Wangari Maathai
items.markingKey: B. The Green Belt Movement mobilised women to plant tens of millions of trees.

items.stem: Explain why Indigenous peoples have become prominent actors in environmental politics.
items.answer: Their territories hold a large share of the world’s remaining biodiversity, they are directly affected by extraction and deforestation, and UNDRIP gives them rights such as FPIC that they use in courts and negotiations.

items.answer: The Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled that Ecuador violated the Kichwa people of Sarayaku’s rights by allowing oil exploration on their land without consultation. items.stem: Under the Kyoto Protocol (1997), which states had legally binding emissions targets?

Only the five largest emitters
Developing states only
All states that ratified it
items.answer: Developed (Annex I) states only
items.markingKey: A. This reflected CBDR; the USA never ratified it and Canada withdrew in 2011.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "climate-induced migration"?
options: Movement of people, temporary or permanent and usually within their own country, driven wholly or partly by sudden or slow-onset climate impacts such as floods, droughts or sea-level rise
The self-set climate pledges that each party to the Paris Agreement (2015) must submit and update every five years
A term (used by the US military advisory board in 2007 and later by the UN) for the way climate change worsens existing risks such as poverty, weak governance and resource competition
The politics of shared water resources, including disputes over dams and allocation on transboundary rivers such as the Nile, Indus and Mekong
items.answer: Movement of people, temporary or permanent and usually within their own country, driven wholly or partly by sudden or slow-onset climate impacts such as floods, droughts or sea-level rise
items.markingKey: A. "climate-induced migration" is movement of people, temporary or permanent and usually within their own country, driven wholly or partly by sudden or slow-onset climate impacts such as floods, droughts or sea-level rise.

items.stem: Define the term "free, prior and informed consent (FPIC)".

items.stem: Briefly describe Amazon deforestation in Brazil (2019–2023) and explain what it reveals about the role of state policy in environmental degradation.
items.answer: Deforestation rose sharply under President Bolsonaro, who weakened enforcement agencies, then fell substantially in 2023 after President Lula restored enforcement and revived the Amazon Fund. The change in rates with a change of government shows that degradation is driven by political choices, not only by markets.

Source B

items.stem:
Source C
Young people around the world have mobilised in unprecedented numbers to demand climate action. They argue that adult leaders have failed them, that the science is clear, and that their generation will pay the price for decisions made today.
— Summary of the youth climate strikes, UN Climate Action Summit, New York (2019) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source C, explain how the source illustrates the idea of intergenerational justice. [4]
items.answer: Young people claim that present decision-makers impose the costs of climate change on future generations who have no say, making fairness between generations a political demand.

items.stem: A student claims: "Pollution is a purely local issue and therefore not a global political challenge." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Many pollutants (greenhouse gases, plastics, mercury, haze) cross borders and require international regimes such as the Minamata Convention (2013).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "International law should create a new legal status for climate refugees."
items.answer: A new status is morally attractive, but regional and bilateral mechanisms are more achievable and may protect more people sooner.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: existing law leaves climate migrants unprotected; Teitiota shows gaps; Pacific states face loss of territory. Arguments against: reopening the 1951 Convention could weaken protections; most movement is internal (Kampala Convention, Guiding Principles); bilateral solutions such as the Falepili Union may be more practical. Supported judgement: A new status is morally attractive, but regional and bilateral mechanisms are more achievable and may protect more people sooner.

items.stem: "Non-state actors have been more effective than states in addressing environmental challenges." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Non-state actors have driven agendas and accountability, but lasting change still depends on state action.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: litigation forced action (Urgenda, KlimaSeniorinnen); NGOs shaped agendas and monitoring; Indigenous groups protect forests. Arguments against: only states can legislate and enforce; activism often fails to change policy (Standing Rock pipeline built); NGOs depend on state cooperation. Supported judgement: Non-state actors have driven agendas and accountability, but lasting change still depends on state action. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The voluntary approach of the Paris Agreement is too weak to address climate change."
items.answer: Paris traded strength for participation; it has shifted expectations but its weak enforcement leaves a large ambition gap.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "tragedy of the commons"?
options: The self-set climate pledges that each party to the Paris Agreement (2015) must submit and update every five years
The right of Indigenous peoples, set out in UNDRIP (2007), to give or withhold consent to projects affecting their lands and resources before they begin
Misleading claims by companies or governments that their products or policies are more environmentally friendly than they really are

Garrett Hardin’s (1968) argument that individuals or states acting in their own rational self-interest will over-use a shared, open-access resource, such as the atmosphere or fisheries, until it is degraded
items.answer: Garrett Hardin’s (1968) argument that individuals or states acting in their own rational self-interest will over-use a shared, open-access resource, such as the atmosphere or fisheries, until it is degraded
items.markingKey: D. "tragedy of the commons" is Garrett Hardin’s (1968) argument that individuals or states acting in their own rational self-interest will over-use a shared, open-access resource, such as the atmosphere or fisheries, until it is degraded.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "climate-induced migration".
items.answer: Movement of people, temporary or permanent and usually within their own country, driven wholly or partly by sudden or slow-onset climate impacts such as floods, droughts or sea-level rise
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: movement of people, temporary or permanent and usually within their own country, driven wholly or partly by sudden or slow-onset climate impacts such as floods, droughts or sea-level rise. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: In Urgenda v the Netherlands (2019), what did the Dutch Supreme Court order the government to do?
items.answer: Cut greenhouse gas emissions by at least 25 per cent from 1990 levels by the end of 2020
items.markingKey: Cut greenhouse gas emissions by at least 25 per cent from 1990 levels by the end of 2020. It was the first case in which a court ordered a state to strengthen climate action on human-rights grounds.

items.stem: Explain why the Montreal Protocol succeeded where climate agreements have struggled.
items.answer: Few industries produced CFCs, substitutes were available and cheap, the benefits were clear and quick, and a multilateral fund paid developing states’ costs; carbon emissions, by contrast, are embedded in every economy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Few industries produced CFCs, substitutes were available and cheap, the benefits were clear and quick, and a multilateral fund paid developing states’ costs; carbon emissions, by contrast, are embedded in every economy. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a refugee and a climate migrant.
items.answer: A refugee has crossed a border owing to a well-founded fear of persecution and is protected by the 1951 Convention; a climate migrant moves because of environmental change and has no specific legal protection, often remaining within their own state.
items.markingKey: A refugee has crossed a border owing to a well-founded fear of persecution and is protected by the 1951 Convention; a climate migrant moves because of environmental change and has no specific legal protection, often remaining within their own state. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why courts have become an important arena for climate activism.
items.answer: When governments are slow to act, activists use constitutional and human-rights law to obtain binding rulings, as in Urgenda (2019) and KlimaSeniorinnen v Switzerland (European Court of Human Rights, 2024).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When governments are slow to act, activists use constitutional and human-rights law to obtain binding rulings, as in Urgenda (2019) and KlimaSeniorinnen v Switzerland (European Court of Human Rights, 2024). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "The tragedy of the commons shows that environmental cooperation is impossible." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Elinor Ostrom showed that communities can manage commons sustainably through local institutions, and regimes like the Montreal Protocol show states can cooperate.
items.markingKey: Elinor Ostrom showed that communities can manage commons sustainably through local institutions, and regimes like the Montreal Protocol show states can cooperate. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why shared rivers can generate interstate tension.
items.answer: Upstream states control flows through dams and irrigation while downstream states depend on them; without agreed allocation, projects such as the GERD are seen by downstream states as threats to national survival.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Tuvalu and sea-level rise shows climate change as a threat to sovereignty.

items.stem: Briefly describe drought in Syria (2006–2010) and explain what it reveals about the contested climate–conflict link.
items.answer: A severe drought drove an estimated 1–1.5 million rural people to cities before the 2011 uprising; some studies linked it to the war, while others argue government policy and repression were far more important. The case is used to argue for a climate–conflict link, but the debate shows the danger of downplaying political causes.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Sarayaku people v Ecuador (2012) shows Indigenous rights and FPIC.
items.answer: The Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled that Ecuador violated the Kichwa people of Sarayaku’s rights by allowing oil exploration on their land without consultation. An Indigenous community used a regional court to establish that states must consult Indigenous peoples before extraction.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Disruptive protest is a legitimate method of environmental activism."
